goal.decided: Our accounting team prints each client's invoice themselves, at that client's tax rate, from the lines they keep in their spreadsheet, without asking a developer. Once it holds, a colleague from accounting on their Linux laptop saves the invoice lines from LibreOffice Calc, runs one command from the guide alone with the client's tax rate, and gets the invoice, with no Python written and no developer asked.

deliverables.name: A colleague from accounting turns the lines saved from their spreadsheet and the client's tax rate into an invoice with one command

decisions.decided: invoicer/cli.py decides how a file of lines saved from a spreadsheet and a tax rate given on the command line become the invoice, and where it goes: the screen, and the default printer with --print; parsing, totals and layout stay with the library
`invoice <lines file> --tax-rate <percent> [--print]`, installed by a [project.scripts] entry `invoice = "invoicer.cli:main"`; main(argv) returns the exit code
a percent as accounting writes it, such as 19 or 7.5 (a trailing % allowed), required on every run, turned into the library's fraction
the form that invoicer.parse_lines reads, one line each `<description>;<price>;<quantity>`, as Calc saves a sheet as Text CSV with ';' as the field separator
invoicer.render's text with the rate given, in the library's default currency
always shown on screen; with --print the same text also goes to the laptop's default printer by `lp`, so accounting checks the totals before it goes out on paper
tests with the standard library's unittest, run by `python3 -m unittest`, needing nothing installed

decisions.about: how the tests call the code
decisions.decided: through main(argv) with a lines file, as the terminal calls it

decisions.about: how tests stand in for lp
decisions.decided: tests put a stand-in `lp` script on PATH in a temporary folder that keeps what it was given; a failing case uses one that exits non-zero, and another has no `lp` on PATH, so no test needs a printer or reaches paper

before showing anything, it refuses a missing or unreadable file, a missing or non-numeric or negative tax rate, a row without three ';'-separated fields (such as a file saved with ',' between fields), a price that isn't a number, and a quantity that isn't a whole number, each with a message naming the row and what to change in Calc or on the command line
a price written with a decimal comma, such as 12,50, is read as 12.50
with --print, where `lp` is missing or fails, such as with no default printer set, it says so after showing the invoice and exits non-zero with a message naming what to set up

deliverables.name: A colleague from accounting installs the command and prints a client's invoice from their spreadsheet by the guide alone

decisions.about: who it's for and what they achieve
decisions.decided: the accounting team on Linux laptops with LibreOffice Calc, who print a client's invoice at that client's tax rate without a developer

one tax rate per invoice, not per line; no list of clients or their rates kept, the rate given each run; plain text in EUR, no PDF or letterhead; no reading of the .ods itself, the lines saved as text first
nothing is held back; the guide says so only where the code leaves a case out
the repository holds no license file and the guide is for staff, so it names none and says it's for internal use
what it does for you, install once, save the lines from Calc, run with the client's rate, get the invoice, fix what it refuses, get help
a real run on a few typical invoice lines at one client's rate, with the command typed and the invoice it gives
you save the sheet's lines as text with ';' between fields, and the command adds the tax at the rate you give and lays out the invoice
how to set a different rate for each client, what to do with a header row or a comma-separated save, that prices with a decimal comma work, and what to do when --print doesn't print

decisions.about: how the laptops get the command
